props.title: A.I. Artificial Intelligence
props.initialSlug: A robot boy's quest to become truly human

sections.content: **A.I. Artificial Intelligence** (2001) represents a fascinating fusion of Stanley Kubrick's cold precision and Steven Spielberg's emotional warmth. Originally developed by Kubrick in the 1970s, the project passed to Spielberg after Kubrick's death, creating a unique hybrid that explores humanity through artificial eyes. The film builds on the robot-child concepts from **Pinocchio** (1940), but ventures into darker territory. Like **Blade Runner** (1982), it asks fundamental questions about consciousness and what makes us human, but through the lens of a child-like android seeking maternal love rather than adult replicants seeking survival.

sections.content: Haley Joel Osment's performance as David anchors the film's emotional core, delivering perhaps cinema's most convincing portrayal of an artificial being learning to process human emotions. The film's structure mirrors David's journey from innocence to experience, with each act growing progressively darker and more complex. The influence of this approach can be seen in later AI-focused films like **Her** (2013) and **I Am Mother** (2019), which similarly explore the emotional capacity of artificial beings.

The film's final act, set in a flooded future Manhattan, remains controversial but represents some of the most haunting imagery in science fiction. This sequence, with its evolved mecha civilization, draws parallels to the posthuman futures depicted in **2001: A Space Odyssey** (1968), suggesting a world where artificial beings have surpassed their creators. SUBHEAD: Visual Effects and World-Building

movies.title: Bicentennial Man
movies.slug: Robin Williams portrays a robot on a 200-year journey to become human, exploring similar themes of artificial evolution

sections.content: The film's seamless blend of practical and digital effects set new standards for depicting artificial beings on screen. Industrial Light & Magic's work on the "flesh fair" sequences and the underwater New York scenes influenced later sci-fi spectacles like **Minority Report** (2002) and **Children of Men** (2006). Particularly groundbreaking was the creation of the mecha characters, which needed to appear simultaneously mechanical and emotionally expressive.
